acidic orange juice matrix degrades DNA of plasmid, plant and yeast origin and that pasteurization procedures affect DNA integrity depending on method and time used.

the acidic nature and pasteurization of orange juice causes a strong degradation and conformation change of plasmid DNA below sizes reported for horizontal gene transfer, and also of yeast and endogenous plant genomic DNA.

acidic conditions and pasteurization procedures have a strong degrading affect on the DNA from transgenic plants, yeast and plasmid DNA and that these conditions are not suitable for the horizontal gene transfer of DNA.

the stability of DNA in the juice matrix and the effect of pasteurization on DNA integrity.
the stability of DNA during the processing of genetically modified orange juice, which may be of interest for the food industry and the regulatory authorities.
the safety of food processing of genetically modified plants and the risk of horizontal gene transmission.

the current standard procedures for pasteurization of orange juice are safe for the consumer.
the risk of horizontal gene flow from transgenic plants to the environment is negligible under realistic industrial processing conditions.
the risk of horizontal gene flow from genetically modified oranges to bacteria in orange juice is negligible under standard industrial conditions.

the risk for horizontal gene transfer is negligible under industrial conditions.

the risk of horizontal gene flow from genetically engineered plants into bacteria is negligible due to the strong degrading effect of the acidic orange juice matrix on DNA.
